candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9999 malware probability, and all 20 top features push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.0063 to +0.0169). The supplied evidence cannot confirm cryptojacking specifically, for three reasons. First, every n-gram has a reported relative frequency of 0.000000, so none can be shown to be a dense or dominant code pattern. Second, no function names, call targets, or locations are listed, so no n-gram can be tied to a routine such as a hash loop. Third, nearly all the n-grams are generic compiler-produced mnemonic pairs (ADD POP, PUSH SUB, SUB MOV, MOV LEA, LEA CALL, CALL ADD, TEST JZ, CMP JL, MOV JZ), which are common in ordinary benign code. The only patterns that weakly hint at bit-manipulation or mixing code are XOR XOR (+0.008826), XOR SHL (+0.007046), XOR MOV (+0.009663), and the XOR/CMOV conditional-move combinations (CMOVZ MOV, XOR CMOVNZ, CMP CMOVZ). These are consistent with hashing or obfuscation routines, but they are equally consistent with unrelated code, so I treat them as suggestive only. The model's malware verdict is strong, but this evidence does not show cryptojacking, as opposed to some other malware class or an unusual compiler or packer signature. The result is therefore inconclusive on cryptojacking and warrants further analysis.
